header.title: Otinel (G): AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Anonymous
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's urn:geste:ed-oting:dipl, from the Geste corpus of chansons de geste, Camps et al. (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Geste corpus of chansons de geste, Camps et al. and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.0215.1: 0215.3 geste can mean both 'heroic story' and 'lineage'. 0215.11 Guennes is Ganelon; cuvers sodiant, 'base hireling', i.e. bought. sodiant is souduiant, 'deceiver, traitor', the usual epithet of Ganelon.
notes.0224.308: 0224.308 'urer aourer' gives two readings side by side ('pray', 'worship'); translated once. 0224.311 parisez: coins struck at Paris (parisis). 0224.314: Roland redeems the sword he has offered at the altar for ten marks.
notes.0234.610: Three lines carry two readings side by side; the first is translated. 0234.610 the second reads 'the knights stand watching them closely'. 0235.618 the second reads 'white' for 'flying' ('a white dove came'). 0235.627 the second reads 'Jupiter the great' for 'stinking Jove'. 0234.613 en croiez: prostrate with arms spread in the shape of a cross.
notes.0258.1317: 0258.1321 oublie: taken as a drink of forgetfulness. 0258.1322 is obscure: mires, 'physicians', presumably the Christians who have treated Otinel; estoutie, 'folly, rashness'.
notes.0226.379: 0227.382 Courouçousse is the name of Otinel's sword, roughly 'the Wrathful'.
notes.0251.1091: 0251.1092 L'une ... l'altre are feminine: the attendants are women. 0251.1097 Seine, the herb's name, means 'healthy' (compare sein, 0251.1100).
notes.0228.427: 0228.431 carries two orderings of the same words ('Ja par vos mais n'ert' and 'Jamais n'ert par vos tenue citez'); translated once.

nodes.text: Whoever wishes to hear a song of fair seeming,
Let him keep quiet and draw near,
And he will hear the flower of the valiant story
Of Pepin's son, the rich and mighty king,
And of the Twelve Peers, who loved one another so much.
So much did they love one another, as we find in reading,
That they never forsook one another all their lives
Until the day on which they died
At Roncevaux, where they were fighting
Against Garsile, the rich and mighty king,
For the wicked Ganelon, the base deceiver,
Sold them there, as some people know.
On that very day when they were fighting,
Thirty thousand and seven hundred died there
They went to the chapel to pray;
The abbot of Saint-Omer sings the Mass.
Charles had a cup of gold brought,
He had it filled to the brim with Paris pennies;
He makes his offering, and then the Twelve Peers.
Roland offered Durendal, his bright blade,
For its ransom he had ten marks given there.
After the Mass they all go to look at
The Saracen who is coming to speak to the king.
The Saracen came in haughtily;
As soon as he sees Charles, he says to him fiercely:
'Lord king,' he said, 'where now is Roland,
I promise you, by my god Tervagant,
Before it is evening or the sun is setting,
I will kill your nephew Roland
With Courouçousse, my sharp sword.'
And the king says: 'May Jesus bring you harm!
If I find Roland, he is dead and done for.'
'Sire,' she said, 'you will go to the battle;
But beware of his sword Durendal:
If you do not defend yourself well with yours,
Never again will a city be held by you.'
The knights look on fiercely.
They sorely fear the blows, which are heavy;
The edges of their swords cut well.
The French throw themselves down in the shape of a cross, toward the East;
They are in great fear for their lord Roland;
They pray earnestly to the Father almighty
That he protect him against the unbeliever,
And that he be neither defeated nor made to yield there.
At these words a dove came flying;
Charles saw it, and all the other people.
The Holy Spirit descends upon Otinel,
Changes his heart at Jesus' command;
Then he speaks two words that are well fitting:
'Roland,' he said, 'draw back there now;
I do not know what thing is counselling me here,
Which has changed my heart and my will.
I renounce Muhammad and Tervagant,
And Apollin and stinking Jove,
[And] then they disarm the courtly knight.
One takes the helmet, the other the steel sword,
They pull the good double-mailed hauberk off his back,
They wash his wounds and put him to bed.
They give him a sweet herb to eat
Which God himself planted in his garden;
Its name is Seine; such a herb is worth prizing.
He soon fell asleep, having great need of it.
When he wakes, he feels quite light,
And was sounder than a plum on the plum tree.
Now let us leave the courtly Ogier here,
Who has plenty of all that he needs.
And Belissent, the fair, the slender.
Never in my life will I love pagans.'
Clarel replies: 'Now I have heard a marvel!
Fool, have you then abandoned your good law?
You are bewitched, and have drunk a draught of forgetting
With which these physicians bring on folly.
Baron, come back and be reconciled.
Make amends to Muhammad for your apostasy
And for the outrage of abandoning his law,
And I tell you truly, without deceit,
